weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular. The same FARM/ChemBERTa-2/GNN ensemble used to generate high-level ADMET training labels is subsequently used as the oracle for evaluating generated molecules. Improvements can therefore reflect learning or exploiting predictor artifacts—especially on optimized, out-of-distribution structures—rather than genuine ADMET improvement. There are no optimization baselines. The paper does not compare against random or matched block replacement, conventional molecular search, SMILES- or graph-based generators, DrugAssist, or even the underlying language model. Comparing each drug only with its mCLM modification cannot establish that the proposed representation or model provides an advantage.

The claimed synthesis guarantee is unsupported. No generated route is executed or independently validated, and there are no measurements of reaction compatibility, success rate, yield, reagent availability, or platform feasibility. Moreover, only 432 of the selected 1,000 tokens are reported as synthesis-aware, while the relationship between this subset and inference-time decoding is unclear.

The reported drug improvements are only changes in predicted binary ADMET scores. The evaluation omits target potency, selectivity, pharmacophore or scaffold retention, chemical validity, drug-likeness, and other safety properties. Consequently, the claim of improving approved drugs or “resurrecting” failed clinical candidates is much stronger than the evidence, since a modification may simply destroy therapeutic activity.

No ablations isolate the effects of modular versus atom/SMILES tokenization, synthesis-aware versus fallback tokenization, GNN block embeddings, function-infused data, vocabulary size, or iterative reasoning. Thus even the reported oracle gains cannot be attributed to the paper’s proposed components.

The out-of-vocabulary experiment does not demonstrate genuine molecular generalization. Having at least one block absent from the 1,000-token vocabulary does not imply an unseen molecule or scaffold, and no generator-level held-out split, corpus deduplication, similarity analysis, or performance breakdown by OOV severity is provided. FDA compounds may also occur in the numerous chemistry training sources.

The aggregate Table 1 results lack exact p-values, confidence intervals, effect distributions, multiple-testing correction, decoding success rates, and numbers of valid outputs per task. Some changes are small, and PGP performance worsens.

Important algorithmic and reproducibility details are missing: block ordering and attachment semantics, candidate retrieval, constrained decoding, prompts, sampling parameters, iteration selection, and stopping rules. Algorithm 1 never updates M to M′ and contains an unbounded loop, while Appendix C contains an unresolved “Appendix ??” reference. No code, model checkpoint, tokenizer implementation, or processed splits are provided.

The manuscript lacks an explicit ethics and dual-use discussion despite proposing function-guided molecular generation coupled to automated synthesis. Overall, the promising concept is not supported by a valid comparative evaluation, making the main scientific claims unreliable.

weaknesses: The principal property-improvement evaluation is circular. The oracle models are validated only by scaffold-split AUC on their original datasets. There is no calibration analysis, uncertainty estimate, applicability-domain check, independent predictor, docking calculation, experimental assay, or prospective validation on the generated distribution.

Data leakage is insufficiently controlled. The corpus aggregates millions of molecules from overlapping public sources, but the paper does not report molecular/scaffold deduplication against the FDA evaluation set or the oracle datasets. Moreover, the allegedly unseen blocks are absent only from the 1,000-token language-model vocabulary; the GNN was pretrained on all approximately 800,000 blocks, so this is not genuine system-level unseen-block evaluation.

The claimed guarantee of automated synthesizability is much stronger than the evidence. No generated molecule is synthesized, let alone on a robotic platform. The analysis assumes every required building block is available and does not establish yields, reaction-condition compatibility, stereochemical fidelity, purification feasibility, or robustness across iterative steps. The less-than-100% Allchemy result also sits uneasily with an unconditional guarantee.

Baseline parity is weak. mCLM is extensively fine-tuned on task-specific, oracle-labeled optimization examples, whereas proprietary LLMs appear to be prompted without comparable adaptation. Prompts, decoding settings, candidate budgets, and selection procedures are omitted. Several natural comparison points—reaction-based generators and matched SAFE/Group-SELFIES or constrained-SMILES models—are not empirically evaluated.

The reported property values appear to be classifier probabilities multiplied by 100, but their calibration and interpretation are not explained. The average relative-improvement metric is unstable for probabilities already near zero or one. There are no confidence intervals, statistical tests, multiple seeds, or clear denominators for several retrospective-synthesis percentages.

Each column of the main property table appears to concern a separately optimized molecule set. Thus it does not show simultaneous multi-objective improvement, nor does it report changes to non-target properties. Target potency, selectivity, scaffold preservation, novelty, diversity, medicinal-chemistry alerts, and other essential drug-quality criteria are also absent.

The claim of rescuing failed clinical candidates is unsupported. Lower predicted DILI scores do not establish reduced human hepatotoxicity, and the generated analogues are not evaluated for retention of BTK or USP1 activity. The paper itself acknowledges that other properties may have been compromised.

The proposed critical-reasoning procedure is essentially an external oracle-guided greedy loop rather than demonstrated internal chemical reasoning. It lacks a quantitative multi-step benchmark and suitable search baselines; the presented pseudocode also never updates M to M' and omits the stated maximum-iteration condition.

Reproducibility remains inadequate: reaction rules and compatibility filters, GNN architecture and graph features, canonical block ordering, data cleaning and splits, generation hyperparameters, and baseline prompts are not fully specified. Code, model weights, and data are only promised after publication, while the main retrosynthesis evaluation depends on proprietary Allchemy software.

Ablations do not isolate several key ingredients, including natural-language supervision, oracle-generated labels, GNN pretraining, vocabulary size, and constrained decoding. The qualitative nearest-neighbor figures provide no aggregate evidence that the learned block space captures functional rather than merely structural similarity.

The discussion omits dual-use and safety considerations despite explicitly advocating automated molecule creation accessible to non-specialists. Overall, the representation is promising, but the circular evaluation and unsupported synthesis and clinical claims prevent the paper from meeting a top-tier acceptance standard.
